title: The Volunteer Paid in Schooling: Loigny, the Salon, and the Maid on the Wall
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Loir and the Volunteers of the West

stops.name: Château-du-Loir, the Christmas birth
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia, Lionel Royer; Wikidata Q1827276); the pin marks the town centre at the church of Saint-Guingalois, not a confirmed birth house, which no consulted source identifies
stops.campa: On Christmas Day 1852 a son is born at Château-du-Loir, a small town on the Loir in the Sarthe, and named Lionel Noël. The house is not recorded anywhere; the pin falls on Saint-Guingalois, the town's old church, the nearest fixed thing of that year still standing. The parish and the battlefield are both within an hour of this font, and between them they will account for nearly everything he paints. He dies outside Paris seventy-three years later, still working on the second of them.
stops.quote: Le peintre Lionel Royer est né en 1852, et meurt en 1926.
stops.quote_source: Notice PM88002005, base Palissy, Ministère de la Culture (POP)
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Guingalois at Château-du-Loir, Sarthe
Wikidata Q1827276, birth record data for Lionel Royer

stops.name: Saint-Péravy-la-Colombe, the mass before the battle
stops.date_confidence: [R] reconstruction: the 1910 painting of the scene is catalogued and dated, the 1870 mass it depicts is not attested in the sources consulted, and fr.wikipedia's articles on the commune and on the battle do not mention it
stops.campa: Tradition among the Volontaires de l'Ouest puts them at mass in the church of Saint-Péravy-la-Colombe before the battle, kneeling in ranks to take communion in the dark. Forty years later Royer paints the scene for the church at Loigny and sets himself among the soldiers with a torch in his hand. Whether the young volunteer stood there in December 1870 or only wished he had, the record does not separate. The church still stands in the village, fourteen kilometres south of the ground the corps charged over later that day.
suggested_refs: The parish church of Saint-Péravy-la-Colombe, Loiret
La Communion des zouaves, Base Palissy PM28000776, for the scene as Royer composed it

stops.name: Loigny-la-Bataille, the colonel finds the sketcher
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle and Royer's presence (fr.wikipedia; loire1870.fr); the wording of Charette's offer survives only through the painter's grandson and is reconstructed dialogue
stops.campa: On 2 December 1870 the Volontaires de l'Ouest, a corps drawn from the old papal Zouaves and attached to the 17th Corps, charge at Loigny under Lieutenant-Colonel Athanase de Charette de La Contrie. Royer is seventeen, under age to enlist and enlisted anyway. In the lulls he draws the field instead of sleeping, and Charette, who is not yet a general and will not be one until 14 January 1871, sees the sketches and offers to pay for the Beaux-Arts. The corps commander that day is Gaston de Sonis, who leads the charge and is broken by it.
suggested_refs: The battlefield and ossuary at Loigny-la-Bataille, Eure-et-Loir
The testimony of Pierre Edouard Torchet, Royer's grandson, on the Charette encounter
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Athanase de Charette de La Contrie'

stops.name: Champagné, the camp of Auvours
stops.date_confidence: [R] for Royer's presence: the battle of Le Mans ran 10 to 12 January 1871 and is attested, but no document places Royer on the field, and fr.wikipedia's account of the battle does not name the Volontaires de l'Ouest among the troops engaged
stops.campa: The retreat carries the army west into the Sarthe. From 10 to 12 January 1871 the battle of Le Mans is fought largely on the ground of the camp militaire d'Auvours at Champagné, ten kilometres east of the city. Royer paints it three years afterwards with all the particulars of a man who was there, and titles the canvas by the first day's date. Nothing in the record puts him on that field. The picture is either a witness's account or a very good reconstruction, and the sources do not decide.
suggested_refs: The camp militaire d'Auvours at Champagné, Sarthe
Bataille d'Auvours, le 10 janvier 1871, Base Joconde notice 000PE009877

segments.name: Rue Bonaparte: a Debt Paid in Schooling

stops.name: Paris, the École des Beaux-Arts
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the sponsorship and the two masters are attested (fr.wikipedia; Musée d'Orsay artist catalogue 21309), but no consulted source gives a matriculation date, so the stop is placed in the year after Loigny
stops.campa: A debt contracted on a battlefield is paid in tuition. Royer enters the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts on the rue Bonaparte and works under Alexandre Cabanel and William Bouguereau, the two men who between them define what a French Salon picture is supposed to look like for thirty years. He learns the finished surface and the staged crowd lit on one figure. Thirty years later the Vercingetorix and the Joan cycle are built out of the grammar of this atelier, without a word of it revised.
suggested_refs: The École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts, 14 rue Bonaparte, Paris
Musée d'Orsay artist catalogue, 'Lionel Royer (21309)'

stops.name: Paris, the first Salon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (fr.wikipedia gives 'à partir de 1874'); the exact opening date of the Salon is not given by consulted sources, so the day defaults to 01
stops.campa: In 1874 Royer shows for the first time at the Salon, then held in the Palais de l'Industrie on the Champs-Élysées, a hall of glass and iron built for the exposition of 1855. He is twenty-one and exhibits as a history painter from the start, which under the Third Republic means painting the nation's memory rather than its present. He will go on showing for nearly forty years and collect a third-class medal, a second-class medal, and a bronze at the Exposition Universelle of 1900.
suggested_refs: The Palais de l'Industrie on the Champs-Élysées, home of the Salon from 1857 to 1897

stops.name: Le Mans, the Auvours canvas enters the Tessé
stops.date_confidence: attested for the painting's date and its presence in the collection (Base Joconde 000PE009877); the year of acquisition is not given by consulted sources
stops.campa: Bataille d'Auvours, le 10 janvier 1871, painted in the year of his Salon debut, enters the Musée de Tessé at Le Mans, twenty kilometres from the field it shows. Base Joconde carries it under notice 000PE009877. The loire1870 summary gives the title as 11 janvier; the catalogue says 10 janvier, and the battle itself ran three days, so the canvas fixes on the first of them. A watercolour of the same years, La cantinière héroïque, is in the Musées du Mans as well, dated only circa 1874.
suggested_refs: Musée de Tessé, 2 avenue de Paderborn, Le Mans
Base Joconde notice 000PE009877

stops.name: Gray, the Musée Baron-Martin
stops.date_confidence: attested for the painting's date, dimensions and collection (fr.wikipedia works list); the acquisition date is not given
stops.campa: La fille de l'hôtesse, an oil of 1875 measuring eighty-two by sixty-six centimetres, goes to the Musée Baron-Martin at Gray in the Haute-Saône, installed since 1903 in the town's château above the river. It is a small picture by a man who will end up making canvases six metres wide. This is the Royer who paints to sell, and nothing in it announces the battlefields or the basilica walls. He is twenty-three and there is no reason yet for anyone to expect either. The museum lists it under his name with the measurements the catalogue gives, and nothing else.
suggested_refs: Musée Baron-Martin, 6 rue Edmond-Pigalle, Gray, Haute-Saône

stops.name: Marseille, Mauresque at the Palais Longchamp
stops.date_confidence: attested for the painting's date and collection (fr.wikipedia works list); the acquisition date is not given, and nothing in the sources places Royer in North Africa
stops.campa: Mauresque, painted 1876, enters the Musée des Beaux-Arts of Marseille in the Palais Longchamp, the water-monument raised to celebrate the arrival of the Durance canal. The subject is orientalist and the handling is Cabanel's: skin and cloth under studio light. No consulted source puts Royer south of the Mediterranean. The Maghreb reaches him the way it reaches most of his generation of Salon painters, through other men's canvases and through a colonial empire already thirty-five years old.
suggested_refs: Musée des Beaux-Arts de Marseille, Palais Longchamp

stops.name: Le Mans, Daphné changée en laurier
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1880 canvas (Base Joconde 00160017326); Diane surprise is undated in the same collection (Base Joconde 000PE009968), a gap the catalogue does not fill
stops.campa: Daphné changée en laurier, dated 1880, joins the Tessé, and with it an undated Diane surprise; Base Joconde numbers them 00160017326 and 000PE009968. Mythology is the other half of a Salon painter's trade, the half that lets him paint a body without a battle around it. Royer works both halves through the 1870s and abandons neither, though the history pictures are the ones the Republic will buy and the schoolbooks will reprint. He turns twenty-eight the year he paints a girl becoming a laurel to escape a god, and no account of him written since mentions the picture.
suggested_refs: Base Joconde notices 00160017326 and 000PE009968, Musée de Tessé

stops.name: Paris, the second grand prix de Rome
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia: 'second premier grand prix de Rome en peinture de 1882'); several English-language summaries drop the word second and imply a Villa Médicis residency that no consulted source supports
stops.campa: In 1882 the École awards Royer the second premier grand prix de Rome for painting. The first goes to Gustave Popelin, for Mattathias refusing to sacrifice to the idols; Royer shares the second rank with Paul Leroy. The distinction matters, because the Villa Médicis and the Roman years belong to the winner of the premier prix alone, and no consulted source puts Royer in Italy at any point in his life. English summaries that say he won the Prix de Rome quietly hand him a residency he never had.
suggested_refs: The 1882 concours for the Prix de Rome in painting, subject: Mattathias refuse de sacrifier aux idoles

stops.name: Paris, the third-class medal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the award year (fr.wikipedia; universdesarts Salon record); the day is not given
stops.campa: The Salon of 1884 gives him a third-class medal, the lowest of the three ranks and the first rung of the official ladder. The system is exact about hierarchy: third class in 1884, second class in 1896, bronze at the Exposition Universelle of 1900. Royer climbs it slowly. The picture that will outlive every medal he was ever given wins him nothing at all in the year he shows it, and the only first prize the record gives him arrives in 1913, thirty-one years after the second grand prix de Rome, for a canvas glued to a wall in the Vosges that no Paris jury could have hung.
suggested_refs: Salon records of the Société des artistes français, 1884
sources: universdesarts.com, Salon record for Lionel Royer

stops.name: Montreal, the colonel in the cathedral
stops.date_confidence: attested for the painting, its date and its location (fr.wikipedia works list, sourced to the cathedral's own PDF); [R] for any presence of Royer in Canada, which no source records
stops.campa: In 1885 Royer paints his old commander: Colonel Athanase de Charette, Commandant des Zouaves Pontificaux. The canvas crosses the Atlantic and hangs in the Basilique-cathédrale Marie-Reine-du-Monde at Montreal, where French Canada keeps the memory of the pontifical Zouaves it sent to Rome. The painter does not sail with it. loire1870.fr calls the picture Le colonel de Charette à Loigny and gives it a height of five metres, and the cathedral's own listing supports neither the title nor the measurement.
suggested_refs: Basilique-cathédrale Marie-Reine-du-Monde, Montreal, collection PDF
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Lionel Royer' (works in public collections, Canada)

stops.name: Chartres, Le Christ au tombeau
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Salon showing of 1887 and the Chartres collection (fr.wikipedia works list; universdesarts Salon record); the date of entry into the museum is not given
stops.campa: Le Christ au tombeau hangs at the Salon of 1887 and afterwards enters the Musée des Beaux-Arts of Chartres, housed in the old episcopal palace against the north flank of the cathedral. Royer is by now a painter the Church commissions and the state collects, which in the France of the 1880s means standing in the middle of a quarrel. He will spend the rest of his working life on Catholic subjects and national subjects at once, as though the two were a single commission.
suggested_refs: Musée des Beaux-Arts de Chartres, ancien palais épiscopal
sources: universdesarts.com, Salon record for Lionel Royer

stops.name: Paris, La Source in the Salon illustré
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication (en.wikipedia); the pin is the canonical Paris coordinate of the corpus, since no address for the publication is given by consulted sources
stops.campa: La Source is published in 1888 in the Salon illustré, the engraved annual that carries the year's pictures into households that will never enter the Palais de l'Industrie. Reproduction is how a Salon painter becomes known under the Third Republic: the canvas hangs for eight weeks, the print circulates for decades. Royer also works as an illustrator for the newspaper supplements, drawing the week's events for readers who take their history in weekly instalments.
suggested_refs: Le Salon illustré, annual engraved edition, 1888

stops.name: Dayton, the Comte d'Adhémar de Cransac
stops.date_confidence: circa 1890 only: en.wikipedia's caption reads 'c. 1890', the Dayton Art Institute collection endpoint returns 404, and this year must not be read as anchored. The pin is the museum's address, supplied by the writer, not by the research pool
stops.campa: A portrait of the Comte d'Adhémar de Cransac, oil on canvas, is dated by the caption on en.wikipedia to about 1890 and hangs in the Dayton Art Institute, in Ohio. How it crossed is not recorded in anything reachable; the museum's own collection search returns a 404 for the object, so the circa is the strongest thing available. Royer paints the French Catholic nobility because that is the world Charette opened to him at seventeen, and the portraits travel further than the painter ever does. Ohio and Montreal each hold a Royer face; he never crosses the Atlantic to see either.
suggested_refs: Dayton Art Institute, 456 Belmonte Park North, Dayton, Ohio

stops.name: Chicago, Cupidon et Psyché at the White City
stops.date_confidence: attested for the painting's date and its showing at the 1893 exposition (fr.wikipedia works list); [R] for Royer's presence, which no source records, and the day is not given
stops.campa: Cupidon et Psyché, painted 1893, sails to the World's Columbian Exposition and hangs in the Palace of Fine Arts in Jackson Park, Chicago, among the plaster palaces of the White City. The painting crosses; the painter, so far as any consulted source records, stays in Paris. The building will outlast the fair, be rebuilt in stone, and become the Museum of Science and Industry. Where the canvas went afterwards is not stated by the sources consulted.
suggested_refs: Palace of Fine Arts, Jackson Park, World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago 1893

stops.name: Orléans, the competition for the cathedral windows
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the competition (fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia both name the concours des verrières de la cathédrale Sainte-Croix d'Orléans); the pin is the cathedral, supplied by the writer, since the research pool gave the place only as France
stops.campa: In 1893 Royer enters the competition for the stained-glass windows of the cathedral Sainte-Croix at Orléans with ten watercolours on the life of Joan of Arc, worked at one tenth of the intended scale. He loses. The windows are never executed to his designs and the ten sheets stay in his studio. It is his first sustained attempt on the subject that will occupy the last twenty-five years of his life, and it fails in the city Joan of Arc relieved in May 1429.
suggested_refs: The concours des verrières of the cathedral Sainte-Croix d'Orléans, 1893

stops.name: Paris, Dreyfus drawn in his cell
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia: Le Petit Journal illustré, no. 218, 20 January 1895); the pin is the paper's historic offices at 61 rue La Fayette, and the only place attested for the making of the drawing is Paris
stops.campa: Number 218 of Le Petit Journal illustré, dated 20 January 1895, carries Royer's drawing of Alfred Dreyfus in his cell before deportation to the Île du Diable. The degradation in the courtyard of the École militaire is two weeks old. Royer has not seen the cell and does not claim to: he draws it in Paris from written accounts, for a paper selling a million copies a week. The picture of the prisoner that a good part of France carries in its head that winter is his.
suggested_refs: Le Petit Journal illustré, no. 218, 20 January 1895
The offices of Le Petit Journal, 61 rue La Fayette, Paris 9e

stops.name: Paris, the second-class medal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the award year (fr.wikipedia; universdesarts Salon record); the day is not given, and the Palais de l'Industrie is under demolition from this same year
stops.campa: The Salon of 1896 gives him a second-class medal. The Palais de l'Industrie is already condemned: demolition begins that year to clear the ground for the Grand Palais and the Petit Palais, and the Salon will spend the rest of the decade without a settled house. Royer's own centre of gravity is shifting too, off the Champs-Élysées and toward two churches, one in the Beauce where he fought and one in the Vosges village where Joan of Arc was born. No further Salon medal appears in the record until 1913, which is also the year the demolished hall's successor gives him his only first prize.
suggested_refs: Salon records of the Société des artistes français, 1896
fr.wikipedia, 'Palais de l'Industrie', on the 1896 demolition
sources: universdesarts.com, Salon record for Lionel Royer

stops.name: Le Mans, the choir of the cathedral painted
stops.date_confidence: attested for the painting's date and collection (Base Joconde 000PE009892); the acquisition date is not given
stops.campa: Le Chœur de la cathédrale du Mans, painted 1896, enters the Tessé under Base Joconde notice 000PE009892. Royer paints the inside of the building whose altar of the Crucifix will one day hold a Christ of his own making. The Sarthe keeps calling him back: born on the Loir, trained in Paris, decorated in Paris, and steadily depositing pictures in the museum and the churches of the département he left at seventeen with a rifle. Five of his works are logged in the Tessé and the Musées du Mans between 1874 and 1896, and the cathedral itself will take one more from him.
suggested_refs: Base Joconde notice 000PE009892, Musée de Tessé

stops.name: Le Mans, the ten watercolours given away
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the gift (fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia); the society's period address is not given by consulted sources, so the pin sits in central Le Mans
stops.campa: In 1897 Royer gives the ten Joan of Arc watercolours, refused at Orléans four years earlier, to the Société historique et archéologique du Maine. A failed competition entry becomes a donation to a learned society in his own province. The sheets survive because he lost. Had the windows been made, the models would have gone into a workshop and out of the record. The cycle he could not build in glass at Orléans he will build in oil at Domrémy, fourteen years later and four times the size.
suggested_refs: Société historique et archéologique du Maine, Le Mans, collections

stops.name: Paris, the Salon of 1899
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exhibition (POP, Base Joconde notice 01160003005; utpictura18 notice 22776); the venue pin is the Champ de Mars, supplied by the writer, because the Palais de l'Industrie named in the research pool had been demolished from 1896 and did not exist in 1899
stops.campa: At the Salon of 1899 Royer shows Vercingétorix jette ses armes aux pieds de César, signed and dated at lower right: the Gaulish chief riding into the Roman camp at Alesia and throwing his weapons down before a seated Caesar. Base Joconde, notice 01160003005, records the showing. Historians note that Vercingetorix certainly did not present himself in arms before Caesar at his surrender, since the Roman guard would have cut him down. The painting says otherwise, at three metres by five.
stops.quote: Les historiens soulignent notamment le fait que Vercingétorix ne s'est certainement pas présenté en armes devant César au moment de sa reddition (il aurait été massacré par la garde romaine).
suggested_refs: POP, Base Joconde notice 01160003005
utpictura18.univ-amu.fr, notice 22776

stops.name: Paris, the bronze medal of the Exposition Universelle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the award (fr.wikipedia; universdesarts exhibition record); the day is not given
stops.campa: The Exposition Universelle of 1900 awards Royer a bronze medal. Fifty million visitors pass through Paris that year, and French history painting of the Cabanel line is already being described, in those same halls, as something finished. The Grand Palais that has replaced the Palais de l'Industrie is a year old, built for this exposition, and the Société des artistes français will move its Salon under that nave in 1901. Royer is forty-seven. He has just made the picture that will be reprinted in French schoolbooks for a hundred years, and the jury of the century's great fair gives him bronze.
suggested_refs: The Palais des Beaux-Arts of the Exposition Universelle, Paris 1900

stops.name: Le Puy-en-Velay, the town buys the canvas
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved: POP/Base Joconde 01160003005 gives purchase by the municipality in 1901 with inventory number 1903.59, while the Musée Crozatier didactic sheet gives 1903 as the purchase year. The day is not given by either
stops.campa: The municipality of Le Puy-en-Velay buys the Vercingétorix, by purchase and not by gift or bequest, and the Musée Crozatier inventories it under number 1903.59. The canvas is three hundred and twenty-one centimetres by four hundred and eighty-two, one of the largest single objects this corpus has tracked. It hangs on the second floor, in the nineteenth-century gallery. Base Joconde dates the purchase to 1901 and the inventory to 1903; the museum's own teaching sheet calls 1903 the purchase.
suggested_refs: Musée Crozatier, Le Puy-en-Velay, inventory 1903.59
The Musée Crozatier didactic sheet on the Vercingétorix
sources: Musée Crozatier didactic sheet (Collège Jules Vallès, Bouge)

stops.name: Le Puy-en-Velay, the rival surrender
stops.date_confidence: the Motte canvas is dated 1886 and attested in the same collection (Musée Crozatier didactic sheet); the stop is dated 1901, the year Royer's surrender joins it, and that placement is the writer's, not a source's
stops.campa: The Crozatier already owns another surrender: Henri-Paul Motte's Vercingétorix se rendant à César, painted 1886, which likewise makes the Gaul taller than the Roman. Two canvases in one provincial museum invert the same defeat the same way, thirteen years apart, by painters who did not collaborate. The museum's own modern label lists the anachronisms in Royer's version, the warhorse too large for Gaulish breeds, the oppidum built like a medieval fortress, and says plainly that the heroic inversion was the convention of the genre.
suggested_refs: Henri-Paul Motte, Vercingétorix se rendant à César, 1886, Musée Crozatier
sources: Musée Crozatier didactic sheet (Collège Jules Vallès, Bouge)

segments.name: Domrémy: the Maid on the Wall

stops.name: Domrémy-la-Pucelle, the village of the Maid
stops.date_confidence: inferred: no consulted source dates Royer's first visit to Domrémy, and the basilica canvases are dated only 1911 to 1918 (Base Palissy PM88002005). The pin is the canonical Domrémy coordinate inherited from Joan of Arc's own file
stops.campa: The village on the Meuse where Joan of Arc was born is by now a pilgrimage site with a building programme. Royer comes into terrain this atlas already holds. Joan of Arc is here, born in the house beside Saint-Rémy. So are the lords of the fief: Joffrey de Bourlémont, who gave the abbey of Mureau the tithes of Domrémy and Greux in 1248, and Pierre Bourlémont, and Pica Bourlémont, whom the Provençal tradition carries off to Assisi. Royer arrives to paint the ground they lived on.
suggested_refs: The birthplace house and church of Saint-Rémy at Domrémy-la-Pucelle

stops.name: Domrémy, the Ladies' Tree
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the tree is attested in Joan of Arc's own trial testimony and is standard in her iconography, but no consulted source documents Royer working at this spot. The pin is inherited byte-identical from the Bourlémont files
stops.campa: The beech the village calls the Ladies' Tree, or the Fairies' Tree, stands on Bourlémont land. Joan named it at her trial, and the witnesses of 1456 remembered the châtelaine Béatrix picnicking beneath it with her husband and her mother-in-law. It is the fixed prop of every painted girlhood of Joan, Royer's included. He is working from the trial record, the same transcript this atlas holds in Joan of Arc's file, and putting it back into pictures for people who will never read a word of it.
suggested_refs: The Arbre des Dames at Domrémy, named in the 1431 trial and the 1456 rehabilitation depositions

stops.name: Chartres, the Lorin glass workshop
stops.date_confidence: the collaboration is attested (fr.wikipedia, 'Lionel Royer' and 'Basilique du Bois-Chenu'); [R] for any visit, which no dated record survives. Charles Lorin directed the studio from 1899, so the collaboration cannot predate that year
stops.campa: Charles Lorin takes over the Chartres glass workshop in 1899, at 46 rue de la Tannerie, and Royer collaborates with him on windows for the basilica at Domrémy. Matching a painted scene to coloured glass draws a painter to the workshop at some point in the work, though no dated visit survives in the sources consulted. Chantal Bouchon reads the result as historicist and vengeful at once: Raphael and Ingres in the drawing, the lost provinces in the intention.
stops.quote: Quoique empreints d'historicisme dans les personnages aux réminiscences raphaélesques et presque ingresques, ces verrières ont une connotation d'appel à la revanche, dans ce lieu de Domrémy si chargé de symbole.
stops.quote_source: Chantal Bouchon, Revue Historique et Archéologique du Maine, quoted in the French Wikipedia article 'Lionel Royer'
suggested_refs: Ateliers Lorin, 46 rue de la Tannerie, Chartres

stops.name: Domrémy, the eight canvases of Bois-Chenu
stops.date_confidence: attested: Base Palissy PM88002005 records eight canvases signed and dated by Royer between 1911 and 1918. The blog date of 1913 for their completion is unsupported, and fr.wikipedia gives no execution dates at all, a contradiction left standing
stops.campa: Base Palissy, notice PM88002005, records eight marouflaged canvases in the basilica of Bois-Chenu, signed and dated by Lionel Royer between 1911 and 1918: the first communion, the arrival at Chinon, Orléans, the coronation at Reims, the last communion, the stake. He paints the life of Joan of Arc through the years in which France fights the war he had been waiting forty years to see. The cycle refused at Orléans in 1893 goes up here instead, on plaster, at full size.
stops.quote: Les scènes de batailles à Orléans devant la forteresse des Tourelles ou à Compiègne offrent à Royer, peintre d'histoire, de donner sa mesure à composer l'enchevêtrement des corps vêtus de cuirasses et des jeux de lances.
stops.quote_source: Chantal Bouchon, Revue Historique et Archéologique du Maine (1998), quoted in the French Wikipedia article 'Lionel Royer'
suggested_refs: Base Palissy notice PM88002005, Basilique du Bois-Chenu
The eight marouflaged canvases in situ at Bois-Chenu
sources: Notice PM88002005, base Palissy, Ministère de la Culture (POP)

stops.name: Chinon, the panel of the recognition
stops.date_confidence: the panel falls within the 1911 to 1918 span attested by Base Palissy PM88002005; 1913 is a placement inside that span, not an attested year. The pin marks the scene depicted, not the painter's location, and is inherited from Joan of Arc's file
stops.campa: One of the eight panels is the arrival at Chinon: the Dauphin hidden among his courtiers, the girl from Domrémy walking to him without hesitation, March 1429. Royer paints the moment this atlas records in Joan of Arc's own file. Yolande of Aragon, who held the Angers court that vetted the girl and paid for her armour, is in the castle that season by every reasonable account, and she is in no painter's composition of the scene, Royer's included. The transcript names the men who tested the girl at Chinon; the paintings keep the Dauphin, the courtiers, and the kneeling figure, and drop the queen of Sicily who financed the whole thing.
suggested_refs: The Château de Chinon, hall of the recognition, March 1429

stops.name: Paris, first prize for history painting
stops.date_confidence: attested by the archival note in Base Palissy PM88002005; the day is not given, and the notice does not say which of the eight canvases took the prize
stops.campa: Base Palissy notes that one of the Domrémy canvases won Royer the first prize for history painting at the Salon of 1913. stops.campa: Another of the eight is the coronation of 17 July 1429: Joan standing armoured beside the altar with her banner, which she said had earned the right to be there. It is the most reproduced Joan image of the nineteenth century and Royer's is one of hundreds. This atlas holds the same scene in Joan of Arc's file, the holy oil of Clovis beside it, and holds Yolande of Aragon, who paid for the road to it. Royer paints the sacring across the years 1911 to 1918, which is to say across a war.

A friend, Louis de Meurville, remembered an open heart of gentleness with everyone, sometimes irritable and impulsive but always ready to help. He has outlived Cabanel by thirty-seven years and Bouguereau by twenty, and the kind of picture all three of them made is by now something the century has finished with.

The plot is not identified in anything consulted, and most sources give only the commune, whose centre lies six hundred metres south of the ground itself. The pictures stay where he put them, in churches and provincial museums across the Sarthe, the Beauce, the Vosges, the Velay, the Haute-Saône, and two cities on the other side of the Atlantic, and they go on being looked at without him. Carl Dreyer works from the same transcript Royer worked from, and cuts to the face where Royer had staged the crowd. A village of a few dozen houses in the Beauce, where a seventeen-year-old volunteer was once seen sketching between charges, keeps more of his work a century and a half later than Paris does. The colonel who paid for his schooling hangs in a cathedral in Montreal, and the general who led the charge hangs six metres wide beside the communion of the zouaves, in a church rebuilt over the ground where both of them went down.
